title: The History of the Term New World

pages.text: The New World is an early modern term. It describes lands in the Western Hemisphere. These lands include the Americas and sometimes Oceania. The term started in the early 16th century during the Age of Discovery.
pages.caption: Sebastian Münster's 1544 map of the New World

evidence.fileTitle: File:Novae Insulae Nova Tabula (New Map of the New World).jpg
evidence.articleCaption: Sebastian Münster's 1544 map of the New World

pages.text: Before this time, European geographers thought the world only included Africa, Asia, and Europe. People later called these three parts together the Old World, expanding the geographical horizon.
pages.caption: Amerigo Vespucci awakens the sleeping America, a late 16th-century illustration depicting Amerigo Vespucci's voyages to the Americas

evidence.articleCaption: Amerigo Vespucci awakens the sleeping America, a late 16th-century illustration depicting Amerigo Vespucci's voyages to the Americas

pages.text: The Florentine explorer Amerigo Vespucci is usually credited for coming up with the term New World. He wrote about lands west of the Atlantic Ocean, concluding that they constituted new continents.
pages.caption: Mundus Novus depicted on the Ostrich Egg Globe in 1504

evidence.articleCaption: Mundus Novus depicted on the Ostrich Egg Globe in 1504

pages.text: Vespucci published his ideas in a pamphlet called Mundus Novus. Other writers like Peter Martyr also used new terms. Christopher Columbus thought the lands were part of Asia.
pages.caption: The 1529 Padrón Real map overseen by Diogo Ribeiro labels the Americas MUNDUS NOVUS "the New World" and traces most of South America and the east coast of North America.

imageProvenance.credit: Diogo Ribeiro (d. 1533)William Griggs (1832–1911) Diogo Ribeiro (d. 1533)William Griggs (1832–1911)

evidence.articleCaption: The 1529 Padrón Real map overseen by Diogo Ribeiro labels the Americas MUNDUS NOVUS "the New World" and traces most of South America and the east coast of North America.

pages.text: Over time, people accepted that these discoveries were a New World and not Asia. Today, people still use the term when talking about historic voyages and early European colonization.

B1-B2.headline: The History of the Term New World

pages.text: The New World is an early modern term that describes the majority of lands in the Western Hemisphere, particularly the Americas, and sometimes Oceania. It was introduced during Europe's Age of Discovery by Italian explorer Amerigo Vespucci.
pages.caption: Sebastian Münster's 1544 map of the New World

evidence.fileTitle: File:Novae Insulae Nova Tabula (New Map of the New World).jpg
evidence.articleCaption: Sebastian Münster's 1544 map of the New World

pages.text: This discovery expanded the geographical horizon of earlier European geographers. Previously, they believed the world included only Africa, Asia, and Europe, which became known collectively as the Old World.
pages.caption: Amerigo Vespucci awakens the sleeping America, a late 16th-century illustration depicting Amerigo Vespucci's voyages to the Americas

evidence.articleCaption: Amerigo Vespucci awakens the sleeping America, a late 16th-century illustration depicting Amerigo Vespucci's voyages to the Americas

pages.text: Vespucci is usually credited with creating the term in his 1503 letter, though similar terms had been used before him. For instance, Peter Martyr used alternative names like the western antipodes shortly after Columbus returned from his first voyage.
pages.caption: Mundus Novus depicted on the Ostrich Egg Globe in 1504

evidence.articleCaption: Mundus Novus depicted on the Ostrich Egg Globe in 1504

pages.text: In his published pamphlet Mundus Novus, Vespucci presented his conclusion that the lands discovered west of the Atlantic Ocean were an entirely different continent rather than the edges of Asia, as Christopher Columbus had asserted.
pages.caption: The 1529 Padrón Real map overseen by Diogo Ribeiro labels the Americas MUNDUS NOVUS "the New World" and traces most of South America and the east coast of North America.

imageProvenance.credit: Diogo Ribeiro (d. 1533)William Griggs (1832–1911) Diogo Ribeiro (d. 1533)William Griggs (1832–1911)

evidence.articleCaption: The 1529 Padrón Real map overseen by Diogo Ribeiro labels the Americas MUNDUS NOVUS "the New World" and traces most of South America and the east coast of North America.

pages.text: Although the geographic relationship between Europe and the Americas remained unclear at first, the concept eventually gained general acceptance. Early maps showed various interpretations, with some connecting Asia to North America while others depicted an open ocean.

Today, the term is still commonly employed when discussing historic spaces and early European colonization, although it has faced criticism for applying a colonial perspective that overlooks the complexity of the world.

C1-C2.headline: Origins and Evolution of the New World Concept

pages.text: Originating during the European Age of Discovery in the early sixteenth century, the term New World denotes the majority of Western Hemisphere lands, specifically the Americas and occasionally Oceania. Italian explorer Amerigo Vespucci introduced the designation through his published writings.
pages.caption: Sebastian Münster's 1544 map of the New World

evidence.fileTitle: File:Novae Insulae Nova Tabula (New Map of the New World).jpg
evidence.articleCaption: Sebastian Münster's 1544 map of the New World

pages.text: This conceptual breakthrough fundamentally reconfigured the spatial paradigms of European geographers, who had previously maintained that the terrestrial world comprised solely Africa, Asia, and Europe—regions subsequently retrofitted with the designation Old World.
pages.caption: Amerigo Vespucci awakens the sleeping America, a late 16th-century illustration depicting Amerigo Vespucci's voyages to the Americas

evidence.articleCaption: Amerigo Vespucci awakens the sleeping America, a late 16th-century illustration depicting Amerigo Vespucci's voyages to the Americas

pages.text: While Vespucci is conventionally credited with popularizing the term via his 1503 letter, antecedents existed. Chronicler Peter Martyr d'Anghiera formulated alternative designations such as the western antipodes following Columbus's initial voyage, reflecting contemporary interpretive friction.
pages.caption: Mundus Novus depicted on the Ostrich Egg Globe in 1504

evidence.articleCaption: Mundus Novus depicted on the Ostrich Egg Globe in 1504

pages.text: Vespucci's Latin publication articulated the explicit hypothesis that western discoveries constituted an entirely distinct continental landmass rather than the eastern periphery of Asia, a proposition that directly contested Christopher Columbus's geographical assertions.
pages.caption: The 1529 Padrón Real map overseen by Diogo Ribeiro labels the Americas MUNDUS NOVUS "the New World" and traces most of South America and the east coast of North America.

imageProvenance.credit: Diogo Ribeiro (d. 1533)William Griggs (1832–1911) Diogo Ribeiro (d. 1533)William Griggs (1832–1911)

evidence.articleCaption: The 1529 Padrón Real map overseen by Diogo Ribeiro labels the Americas MUNDUS NOVUS "the New World" and traces most of South America and the east coast of North America.

pages.text: Early sixteenth-century cartography mirrored this evolving understanding while retaining elements of classical authority. While some cartographers depicted open oceanic expanses between Asia and the Americas, others persisted in merging northern Asian landmasses with North America.

Contemporary usage of the term remains prevalent in historiography concerning European colonization, notwithstanding scholarly critiques that argue the terminology imposes a problematic colonial framework which obscures historical and geographic complexity.
